description: Antigone buries her brother against the orders of King Creon. Between city law and family duty, Sophocles poses a conflict that has never aged.

hero.hook: A young woman, a forbidden tomb, and the law of the city that trembles.

blocks.text: After the  War, two brothers died killing each other: **Eteocle**, defender of Thebes, and **Polyneices**, attacker. The new king, **Creon**, uncle of Antigone, orders one to be honored and the other left unburied. **Antigone**, daughter of Oedipus and sister of the two brothers, refuses. She buries the body. Sophocles makes it one of the most discussed plays in Western theater. [[Seven Against Thebes]]

The conflict is clear: on one side the **written law** of the city, on the other the duties towards the dead and the family. Nobody is completely wrong. This is why the play is still debated, from Athenian theaters to modern philosophy classes.

Antigone is the daughter of **Oedipus**, king of Thebes who, without knowing it, killed her father and married her mother. His family is already cursed. In Thebes, each generation pays the previous one. Creon, uncle who became king after the civil war, wants to restore order. For him, a traitor does not deserve funeral rites. To honor Polyneices is to betray the saved city.

blocks.caption: Antigone facing Creon: two justices who do not speak the same language.

blocks.text: But leaving a body without a grave also means offending the gods of the dead, including , the abode of souls in Greek mythology. Antigone acts in the name of a law older than the decree of the day. She is not fighting for power. She fights for a simple gesture: covering a body with earth, as family piety dictates. [[Hades]]

sections.title: The legacy of Oedipus still weighs

blocks.text: Antigone does not act in secret for long. She assumes. Facing Creon, she opposes the . On the one hand, what seems right by nature or by the gods. On the other, positive law, the human decree of the sovereign. Her sister **Ismène** hesitates, frightened. Antigone chooses the act. She accepts being punished for remaining faithful to what she holds sacred. [[Natural law vs. positive law]]

In the 20th century, the play by **Anouilh**, in 1944, takes up Antigone under the Nazi Occupation. The public reads it as resistance to authority. Sophocles was more ambiguous: Creon also has his reasons, and the play does not clearly decide.

blocks.caption: Antigone buries Polyneices: a simple gesture, a war of values.

sections.title: To disobey is also to say “I”

blocks.text: Creon sentences Antigone to be buried alive. His son **Haemon**, Antigone's fiancé, begs him. The king is stubborn. It is the , the excess that pushes a man to believe that he is above the gods. When he finally gives in, it is too late. Antigone, Haemon, then Queen **Eurydice** die. Creon remains alone, broken. [[Hybris in Greek tragedy]]

The  turns everything on its head. It is the sudden change of situation towards the outcome. Creon wanted to save the city. He destroys his own house. Sophocles shows that power that is deaf to its limits becomes a catastrophe. Public order without measure ends up producing the chaos it claimed to avoid. [[adventure]]

sections.title: Creon lasts too long: the hubris of power

blocks.text: Antigone is not only a heroine of disobedience. Creon is not just a tyrant. The play confronts two goods: public order and family piety. **Hegel**, a 19th century German philosopher, saw this as a conflict of legitimate rights. Each side is right according to its principle. Modern readings see civil courage, the question of gender, the tension between State and conscience.

**Antigone** asks an ever-present question: what to do when the law of the city offends what we hold sacred? Sophocles refuses the simple answer. It shows the price of both camps, without exonerating anyone.

sections.title: A tragedy of values, not a slogan
